name: Annapurna Base Camp
description: Multi-day teahouse trek into a 4,130m glacial amphitheater ringed by 7,000m+ peaks.
travel: Fly Bangkok-Kathmandu (~3.5h), then flight or bus to Pokhara, then a 7-12 day teahouse trek starting from Nayapul.

peak.why: Stable weather, clearest mountain views; spring rhododendron blooms, autumn is the driest air of the year.

mid.why: Shoulder season - warmer/hazier pre-monsoon in May, early post-monsoon clearing in September.

low.why: Doable with proper gear but very cold (down to -20C at base camp) and snowy; fewer crowds.

unavailable.why: Monsoon: leeches, landslide risk, and clouded-out views most days.

name: Samaesan
description: Navy-run wreck diving off Sattahip: the sunken warship HTMS Khram serves as an artificial reef, plus the extreme-depth Samaesan Hole for technical divers.
travel: ~2.5-3.5h drive from Bangkok to Sattahip/Samaesan. Day-trip dive boats depart from piers in Samaesan town; also bookable as a weekend liveaboard/package.

peak.why: NE monsoon dry season: calmest seas and clearest visibility, the high season for Gulf of Thailand diving out of Sattahip.

mid.why: Shoulder months as the SW monsoon transitions in and out: still decent visibility, fewer crowds.

low.why: SW monsoon: choppier seas and reduced visibility (roughly 3-10m), but the eastern seaboard is sheltered from the worst of it so trips still run.

name: Koh Tao
description: Small Gulf of Thailand island famous as one of the world's most popular and affordable places to get PADI certified, with dive sites like Chumphon Pinnacle, Sail Rock, White Rock, and the scuttled HTMS Sattakut wreck.
travel: Overnight bus/train + ferry from Bangkok (~10-12h total), or fly Bangkok to Koh Samui/Chumphon then ferry (~2-3h) to Koh Tao pier.

peak.why: Calmest seas and best visibility of the year (often 25-30m), plus peak whale shark season at sites like Chumphon Pinnacle.

mid.why: SW monsoon roughens the west coast, but Koh Tao is sheltered and boats simply shift to the calmer east side; Sep-Oct in particular often rivals peak-season visibility with far fewer divers.

low.why: NE monsoon: the roughest seas and lowest visibility of the year (sometimes under 10m), and some exposed west-coast sites become inaccessible - but sheltered sites like Twins and White Rock keep running most days, so diving doesn't actually stop.

name: Mount Kinabalu
description: Southeast Asia's highest peak (4,095m) in Kinabalu Park, Borneo — a two-day guided trek via Laban Rata to Low's Peak for sunrise above the clouds.
travel: Fly Bangkok to Kota Kinabalu (~3.5h direct), then ~2h drive to Kinabalu Park HQ / Timpohon Gate to start the climb.

experiences.title: Two-day summit trek to Low's Peak

peak.why: Sunniest, clearest skies of the year — best odds of an unobstructed sunrise from Low's Peak, though permits book out 6-9 months ahead.

mid.why: Dry season continues with good trail conditions and steadier permit availability than the Feb-Apr rush.

low.why: Tail end of the monsoon — trails often still wet underfoot, but climbable with fewer crowds.

unavailable.why: Peak monsoon — heaviest rain, slippery trails, and the highest risk of summit closure for safety.

name: Bali
description: Indonesia's most-visited island, a mix of Ubud's rice terraces and temples, Uluwatu/Canggu/Seminyak's beaches and surf, and volcanic landscapes around Batur and Agung.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok (BKK/DMK) to Denpasar (DPS), ~4h20m.

peak.why: Core dry season: sunny, low humidity, and the least rain of the year (Denpasar/Ubud both bottom out around 15-40mm in Aug) — best all-around conditions for rice terraces, temples, and beaches.

mid.why: Shoulder dry season transitioning in/out of the wet months: still mostly sunny with occasional showers, warmer and more humid than peak, noticeably fewer crowds.

low.why: Wet season, wettest Dec-Feb (Ubud ~280-400mm/month vs <100mm in dry season): frequent afternoon downpours and high humidity, with brief flash flooding in low-lying spots like Canggu/Seminyak/Kuta that drains within an hour or two. Temples, rice terraces, and beaches stay open, though some hiking/trekking tours pause during storms.

name: Memories Beach
description: Wide sandy beach break in the Pakarang area north of Khao Lak, on the Andaman coast — beginner-friendly white-water rollers plus nearby reef breaks at Cape Pakarang for more experienced surfers.
travel: Fly Bangkok to Phuket (~1.5h) then drive/taxi north to Khao Lak (~1-1.5h), or direct minivan/bus from Bangkok (~9-10h).

peak.why: SW monsoon at its strongest: most consistent swell of the year, with July often cited as the single best month.

unavailable.why: Dry season: prevailing easterly wind leaves the coast sheltered by the mountains and seas go flat/glassy — no swell for surfing (this is peak season for diving/beach tourism instead).

mid.why: Monsoon building up and tapering off: smaller, less consistent swell than peak, but still surfable and less crowded.

name: New Zealand
description: A self-drive loop through the South Island's mix of alpine lakes, fjords, and glaciers — Christchurch, Kaikoura's coast, Queenstown, Milford Sound, and the Franz Josef/Fox glaciers, with side trips north to Rotorua and Tongariro possible on a longer North Island extension.
travel: No direct flights from Bangkok; connect via Singapore or another hub to Christchurch (CHC) or Auckland (AKL), total travel time roughly 20-24h door-to-door including the layover.

peak.why: Southern Hemisphere summer: warmest temps (19-23C), longest daylight, and all alpine roads (Milford Road, Lindis Pass, Crown Range) clear of snow with no chain requirement — best all-around driving conditions, though also the most crowded and expensive time to book.

mid.why: Autumn and spring shoulder seasons: mild weather (13-19C) and noticeably fewer crowds/lower prices. Roads are generally clear, but May and October can see early/late alpine snow, and Nov falls inside the Jun-Nov window where Milford Road legally requires carrying snow chains as a precaution.

low.why: Winter: cold (1-10C) with short daylight hours. Snow chains are a legal requirement for the Te Anau-Milford Sound section and common on Lindis Pass/Crown Range, and the Milford Road can see temporary night closures or gate closures during active avalanche-control periods. Roads reopen once conditions are managed and self-drive trips still run, just with more caution, delays, and route flexibility needed.

name: Faroe Islands
description: 18 volcanic islands strung between Iceland and Norway - sheer sea cliffs, grass-roof villages, and a dense network of ridge and coastal hikes (Drangarnir, Lake Sorvagsvatn/Traelanipa, Mulafossur, Kalsoy) packed into a tiny, endlessly green archipelago.
travel: No direct flights from Bangkok to the Faroes; fly Thai Airways or SAS direct BKK-Copenhagen (~10.5-11h), then Atlantic Airways or SAS on to Vagar (FAE, ~2h15m) - roughly 16-20h door-to-door including the Copenhagen layover. Vagar airport is ~45min by road/tunnel from Torshavn.

peak.why: Summer: mildest temps (9-13C), near-midnight sun with 16-20+ hours of daylight, and all hiking trails, ferries (including the seasonal Mykines puffin ferry) and tour operators running at full capacity - the most reliable weather window, though also the busiest and priciest (book cars/hikes/Mykines permits well ahead).

mid.why: Shoulder season: trails reopen and green up through April, the seasonal Mykines puffin ferry starts running in May as birds return, and daylight stays generous (10-18h) with noticeably fewer crowds than summer; September still has workable conditions before autumn storms set in.

low.why: Winter half of the year: daylight drops to as little as 5-7h in Nov/Dec, rain and wind pick up substantially with frequent gales, the Mykines ferry stops running for the season, and exposed ridge trails (Slaettaratindur, Kallur Lighthouse) are frequently icy, snow-covered or genuinely impassable, especially in January. Roads and the subsea tunnel network (built partly to bypass weather-dependent ferries) stay open, and trips still run with more layers, flexibility and caution rather than stopping outright.

name: Phu Soi Dao National Park
description: Multi-day trek to Thailand's highest pine savanna meadow (ลานสน) on the Laos border, famous for the rainy-season dok-ngon-nak wildflower bloom and cold-season sea-of-mist views from a 2,102m summit.
travel: Fly Bangkok-Phitsanulok (~1h) or overnight bus/train, then ~2.5h drive to the Huai Muen (Mo Sai Wan) ranger checkpoint in Nam Pat district, Uttaradit; trek starts from there.

peak.why: Cool, clearer season: pleasant trekking weather Oct-Nov, coldest air Dec-Jan with dramatic morning sea-of-mist over the pine meadow; the most popular window and where the DNP online tent quota fills fastest.

mid.why: Rainy season, but this is when the park's signature dok-ngon-nak (Cornukaempferia) wildflower carpets the summit meadow in bloom; trails are muddier and rain is frequent, though the park is fully open and busy with flower-chasers.

unavailable.why: DNP closes the summit meadow/trekking zone park-wide each dry season (roughly mid-Jan through June 30) to let vegetation recover and prevent wildfires; no trekking permits are issued and the trail is physically closed during this window.

name: Jeju Island
description: Volcanic island off South Korea's south coast, home to Hallasan (South Korea's highest peak) and a UNESCO-listed volcanic landscape of lava tubes, crater lakes, and coastal cliffs.
travel: No direct flights from Bangkok; connect via Seoul Incheon (BKK-ICN ~5.5hr, ICN-CJU ~1hr) on Korean Air, Jeju Air, or similar, or via Seoul Gimpo with a domestic Jeju leg — total door-to-door travel roughly 8-10hr each way.

experiences.title: Hike Hallasan to Baengnokdam crater lake

peak.why: Autumn: dry, settled weather with the clearest air of the year and the most reliable Baengnokdam summit views, plus fall foliage on the crater slopes peaking late October to early November - early November can already mix the first snow dustings with the last colour. The most popular window; reserve the Seongpanak or Gwaneumsa permit as early as you can.

mid.why: Late spring: the mildest hiking temperatures of the year, with royal azaleas on the upper slopes in May and most of the winter snow gone (patches linger near the summit into April). The catch for the crater view is spring fog and strong high-altitude winds, which frequently leave Baengnokdam socked in even on an otherwise clear day.

low.why: Two off-seasons. December-March is full winter on the summit trails: snow and ice from around 1,000m up, crampons required (basic ones sold at the trailheads), severe windchill, and more frequent closures of the summit section for high wind or heavy snow - but both routes still run by reservation and the snow-covered crater is a spectacular, if demanding, hike. June-September is the monsoon and typhoon season: heaviest rain June-July, heat and humidity at the trailhead, near-daily afternoon thunderstorms, and typhoon risk in August-September, with the summit usually lost in cloud.

peak.why: The two mild, low-humidity windows with the best light on the coast. April-May: warm, settled, and the flower season - canola through April and cherry blossom in early April along the coastal roads and around Seongsan Ilchulbong. October-November: clear skies, cool 15-25C walking weather, low humidity, and silver pampas grass along the cliff-top and volcanic sections; the southern-coast light in October is exceptional. Typhoon risk has faded by mid-October.

mid.why: Shoulder months. March: the winter monsoon is easing and the first canola opens in the southwest, but it is still cool and blustery on exposed cliffs and headlands. June: warm and green, but humidity climbs and the jangma rainy season arrives in bands from around the third week. September: heat and humidity linger and it is the peak of Jeju's typhoon season (early-to-mid September the highest risk), though a settled late-September spell - once the domestic summer crowds have gone - can be superb.

low.why: December-February: the northwesterly winter monsoon batters the exposed coast, cold is wind-chill driven (air 3-10C but feels far colder on the cliffs), skies are often grey, steps at viewpoints like Seongsan Ilchulbong get frosty and slippery, and winter sunrises are frequently clouded out - the Olle trails stay open but coastal walking is raw. July-August: hot and very humid with almost no shade on the coastal sections (the guided Olle walks are suspended for the heat), the tail of the rainy season runs into July, and it is the peak of domestic holiday crowds.

name: Maldives
description: Chain of ~1,190 coral islands across 26 atolls in the Indian Ocean - overwater villas, house reefs, and channel (kandu) dives famous for manta rays, whale sharks, and grey reef sharks.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok (BKK) to Male (MLE), ~4.5h, then a seaplane, domestic flight, or speedboat transfer out to the resort island (or board a liveaboard in Male).

peak.why: Northeast monsoon dry season: clear skies, calm seas, 8-9h sunshine and the least rain of the year (Jan-Feb driest), with reef visibility of 25-40m. Also the most crowded and expensive window, peaking over Christmas-New Year; April is the hottest month as the dry season tails off.

mid.why: Monsoon transition months: more humidity and short, heavy showers or brief squalls, but still plenty of sun, easing visibility and noticeably lower prices and crowds than peak season.

low.why: Southwest monsoon wet season: stronger winds, rougher seas and the wettest months (Sep-Oct ~240mm), with overcast spells and visibility dropping to roughly 10-20m from plankton blooms. Diving and resorts run all year, and those same blooms drive peak manta and whale shark aggregations at Hanifaru Bay / Baa Atoll, biggest Aug-Oct.

name: Cebu
description: Long, narrow Visayan island whose southwest coast around Moalboal is a diving hub - a year-round sardine run and sea turtles off Panagsama Beach and the Pescador Island wall - with the Kawasan Falls canyoneering route through turquoise river pools just up the coast at Badian.
travel: Fly Bangkok to Cebu (Mactan-Cebu, CEB), ~3.5h direct or via Manila, then ~2.5-3h by car/van southwest across the island to Moalboal.

peak.why: Amihan dry season: calm seas, little rain (driest Feb-May) and 20-30m+ visibility on the Panagsama reef and Pescador Island wall. Philippine summer Mar-May is the busiest and priciest stretch.

mid.why: Transition into the dry season: habagat rains ease and visibility recovers, and it's the least crowded month of the year with noticeably lower lodging prices.

low.why: Habagat southwest monsoon: more frequent showers, visibility down to ~10-20m, and the core of the typhoon window (highest risk Aug-Oct). Moalboal's west-coast position is relatively sheltered so diving runs year-round, but boat days and transfers can be disrupted by passing storms; the sardine school itself is resident and present every month.

peak.why: Dry season: sunny, stable weather and low, clear turquoise water in the Kanlaob canyon - the most reliable window. Mar-May (Philippine summer, Holy Week) is the most crowded.

mid.why: Rains tapering off but late-season storms are still possible in the Visayas; generally good conditions with fewer crowds, just check for closures after heavy rain.

low.why: Rainy season: the canyon is at its lushest, but heavy upstream rain raises the river fast and the LGU closes the route during heavy rain and typhoon warnings (flash-flood risk). Tours still run on clear days, so build in schedule flexibility.

name: Sydney
description: Australia's largest city, built around one of the world's great natural harbours - the Opera House and Harbour Bridge, ocean beaches like Bondi and Manly, the Bondi-to-Coogee clifftop walk, and the Blue Mountains an easy train ride west.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok (BKK) to Sydney (SYD), ~9h.

peak.why: Autumn and spring shoulders: mild, settled weather (highs ~20-26C), lower humidity and among the driest months (Sep-Oct), ideal for the Bondi-to-Coogee coastal walk, harbour, and Blue Mountains day trips - fewer crowds and lower prices than summer. Early March and October are the sweet spots.

mid.why: Summer: warm to hot (highs ~26C, heatwave spikes past 40C) and humid with afternoon thunderstorms, but the warmest sea and full beach and harbour-swim season. Busiest and most expensive time - NYE fireworks and Christmas/January school holidays - and February begins the wettest stretch of the year.

low.why: Late autumn into winter: coolest (daytime ~17-19C, nights ~8C) with the shortest daylight, and May-June are the two wettest months of the year with heavy east-coast-low downpours. Everything stays open, it's the cheapest low season, and whale watching runs off the coastal cliffs (May-Nov).

name: Melbourne
description: Australia's coffee-and-culture capital on the Yarra - Victorian arcades and graffitied laneways, a dense bar and restaurant scene, world sport at the MCG and Melbourne Park, and the gateway to the Great Ocean Road and Yarra Valley.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok (BKK) to Melbourne (MEL), ~9.5h.

peak.why: Autumn's settled, mild weather (highs ~18-24C; March is the driest month of the year, plus the F1 Grand Prix and the start of the Comedy Festival) and warm, event-packed mid-to-late spring - Spring Racing Carnival, Melbourne Cup, footy finals - though spring is wetter and windier than autumn. Shoulder-season crowds and prices.

mid.why: May is a mild autumn shoulder - dry, quiet, with the last of the foliage - but cool (highs ~17C) and can already feel wintry. December-February is the warmest and most event-packed stretch (Australian Open, festivals, bay beaches at St Kilda and the Mornington Peninsula), but prone to sharp 35-40C+ heat spikes and abrupt cool changes, and it's the busiest and most expensive window.

low.why: Winter and the raw edge of early spring: cold for Australia (July highs ~13-14C, nights ~6C), grey and drizzly, with September both chilly and one of the wettest months. The city's indoor life - laneway bars, galleries, coffee, footy at the MCG - carries on regardless, it's the cheapest season, and the Victorian snowfields (Mt Buller ~3h, Falls Creek ~4.5h) run roughly June to early October for a snow day out.

name: New York City
description: The five-borough metropolis - Manhattan's skyline and museums (the Met, MoMA), Central Park, Broadway, and a food and neighbourhood scene spanning Brooklyn, Queens and beyond.
travel: No nonstop from Bangkok; one stop (via Tokyo, Doha or a European hub) to New York (JFK/EWR), ~18-20h door to door.

peak.why: Spring and early fall: mild, comfortable temperatures (~15-25C), lower humidity, long days, cherry blossoms in Central Park in spring and peak foliage in the parks in late October. The consensus best window.

mid.why: Jul-Aug is hot and humid (~28-30C) but the city lives outdoors - free concerts, rooftop bars, Shakespeare in the Park - at peak crowds and prices. Late Nov and Dec are cold but the city is at its most festive.

low.why: Deep winter: cold (highs ~3-5C, lows below freezing) with snow, slush and biting wind, and March still raw. Everything stays open and indoor draws - museums, Broadway - are unaffected; hotel rates are at their lowest, dropping ~30% after New Year's.

peak.why: The full holiday city: the lit Rockefeller Center tree, department-store window displays, holiday markets (Union Square, Columbus Circle, Bryant Park's Winter Village), outdoor ice rinks and Times Square on New Year's Eve - all live at once, at the cost of the year's thickest crowds and highest hotel prices.

low.why: Shoulders of the season: Bryant Park's Winter Village and rinks open from late October and the Union Square market from mid-November, but the Rockefeller tree isn't lit until early December; in January the tree stays lit into the first week and the Winter Village rink runs on, but the markets and window displays come down and the crowds thin.

unavailable.why: The Rockefeller tree, holiday markets and window displays are only installed from mid-November through early January - none of it exists the rest of the year (Bryant Park's Winter Village rink lingers into early March, but that alone isn't the holiday season).

name: Okinawa
description: Japan's subtropical southern island chain - white-sand beaches, the coral-rich Kerama Islands and the Blue Cave for diving and snorkelling, Ryukyu-kingdom castles, and humpback whales offshore in winter.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok to Naha (OKA), ~4.5h, or via a mainland Japan hub.

peak.why: Okinawa's calm, typhoon-free diving window. April-June: settled seas as the drift-diving season opens, visibility excellent (clearest late April and late June), water warming from ~24C into the high 20s - caveats are Golden Week crowds around late April to early May and the tsuyu rains from early May (rain doesn't cancel dives, only wind and waves do). October-November: typhoons have cleared, water still 25-27C, visibility back to 30m+, November has the most settled weather of the year, and crowds and prices are low.

mid.why: Winter: the clearest water of the year on the Kerama reefs (often 30-40m as the plankton dies back), plus humpback whales around the Keramas and hammerheads off Yonaguni from January to March. But it's the coldest water (~19-22C, a 5-7mm wetsuit or drysuit), the air and wind are cold, and the northerly monsoon cancels some boat days (south-facing sites are the fallback); a few small operators cut back their hours. The quietest and cheapest season - good diving for the well-prepared.

low.why: Midsummer and the peak of typhoon season. Water is at its warmest (28-30C) and diving carries on, but visibility drops to ~20-25m in the summer plankton bloom, and August-September storms are frequent enough to ground dive boats and inter-island ferries for days at a time (September carries the highest typhoon risk). It's also the most crowded and most expensive stretch, over the school holidays and Obon.

peak.why: Humpbacks gather around the Kerama Islands to breed; boats from Naha and Tomari run daily with 90%+ sighting rates, best late January through February.

low.why: Shoulders of the migration: the first whales arrive in late December and stragglers linger into early April, so tours still run but sightings are less reliable.

unavailable.why: The humpbacks are up in their northern feeding grounds - no whale-watching tours operate in Okinawa outside the roughly December-April breeding season.

peak.why: Late autumn through winter into early spring: mild (~18-22C), dry, low humidity and essentially no typhoons - the comfortable window for gusuku castle ruins, coastal viewpoints (Cape Manzamo, Kouri Island) and exploring Naha on foot. Okinawa's deep-pink kanhizakura cherry blossoms bloom from mid-January, peaking around late January at spots like Nakijin Castle - the earliest sakura in Japan - and it's the low-price off-season since it isn't beach weather.

mid.why: April is warm and mostly dry and good for sightseeing, but Golden Week at its end brings a domestic-travel crush. October eases back into comfortable conditions as the heat and typhoon risk fade, though early in the month it can still be hot, humid and storm-prone.

low.why: The tsuyu rainy season (mid-May to late June) is hot and very humid with frequent heavy downpours; July-September is hotter still (32-34C, draining for castles and outdoor sites), the peak of typhoon season (Aug-Sep storms can close attractions and ground flights), and the most crowded domestic-holiday stretch. Indoor draws like the Churaumi Aquarium and the summer Eisa festivals are the exceptions.

peak.why: Sea open (the umi-biraki opening ceremonies are in March) and warm - about 23C in April rising to ~27C - with the lowest typhoon risk of the swimming year, few crowds outside Golden Week (late April to early May), and box jellyfish not yet a factor before June. October is the standout: water still ~27C, typhoons easing, and prices and crowds drop once the Japanese school holidays end in the first week.

mid.why: Peak summer: the warmest water of the year (29-30C) and every beach facility fully open, but also the peak of typhoon season (August-September storms can close beaches and ground flights for days), the peak of box-jellyfish season (swim inside the netted areas at managed beaches - stings outside them can be serious), fierce heat and humidity, and the most crowded and expensive stretch over the school holidays and Obon.

low.why: Managed beaches close their swimming operations at the end of October, so from November there are no lifeguards and no jellyfish nets. Water cools from ~25C in early November to ~21C by February and the air turns cool (15-19C) - fine for beach walks, beachcombing and a warm-day paddle, but not a swimming season for most.

name: Cappadocia
description: Volcanic tableland of 'fairy chimney' rock spires, cave churches and cliff-carved towns like Goreme - and the launch site for the hundreds of hot-air balloons that fill the sunrise sky most mornings.
travel: Fly Bangkok to Istanbul (~10h), then a domestic flight to Kayseri (ASR) or Nevsehir (NAV), ~1.5h, then ~45min-1h by road to Goreme.

peak.why: Spring and autumn: mild mornings (~15-25C), settled air and clear skies give an 85%+ chance flights actually launch, with the best sunrise light and only moderate crowds - the consensus best window.

mid.why: Peak summer has the highest launch rate of the year (cancellations under 10%) thanks to calm, stable mornings, but it's the busiest and priciest time with hot, hazy afternoons - balloon slots and cave hotels book out months ahead.

low.why: Winter and its shoulders: the snow-dusted fairy chimneys are at their most striking, but fog, snow and sustained wind ground flights on roughly 35-50%+ of mornings (January the worst; March notably windy). Flights still run whenever the civil-aviation authority clears the morning - budget 2-3 mornings to be safe - and it's the cheapest, quietest season.

name: Egypt
description: From the Giza pyramids and the Grand Egyptian Museum through Luxor's temples and tombs and a Nile cruise to Aswan - and, on the other side of the country, world-class reef and wreck diving in the Red Sea.
travel: No direct flight from Bangkok; one stop via a Gulf hub (Doha, Dubai, Abu Dhabi) to Cairo (CAI), ~12-14h total. Red Sea resorts (Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh, Marsa Alam) have their own airports, reached via a Gulf hub or a domestic hop from Cairo.

peak.why: Late October to February: warm, dry days and cool nights across Cairo, Luxor and Aswan - the comfortable window for tombs, temples and a Nile cruise. December-January is the mildest but also the most crowded and expensive.

mid.why: March-April: still warm rather than hot and noticeably quieter, but the Khamsin can bring hot, dust-laden winds and occasional sandstorms, mainly around Cairo and Aswan.

low.why: May-September: Upper Egypt is punishingly hot - Luxor and Aswan regularly hit 41C+ and Jun-Aug is often called unbearable. Sites and cruises still run and it's the cheapest, least crowded time, but sightseeing means being out at dawn and indoors by midday.

peak.why: Spring and autumn: water a comfortable 24-28C, calm seas, and peak shark season on the offshore reefs (Brothers, Daedalus, Elphinstone) - best hammerhead and oceanic-whitetip numbers Oct-Nov. The favourite windows for conditions versus crowds.

mid.why: Summer: warmest water of the year (up to 30C) and calm conditions for the wrecks (Thistlegorm) and reefs, but air temperatures hit 35-40C on land and it's the busiest, priciest stretch.

low.why: Winter: coldest water (21-23C, a 5-7mm wetsuit or drysuit) and the strongest winds, and many offshore liveaboards pause in January. Sheltered day-boat diving from Sharm el-Sheikh and Hurghada runs all year, and it's the quietest, cheapest season.

name: Seattle
description: Pacific Northwest port city between Puget Sound and Lake Washington - Pike Place Market, the Space Needle and a deep coffee, music and food scene, with Mount Rainier, Olympic and North Cascades national parks all in day-trip range.
travel: No nonstop from Bangkok; one stop via a North Asian hub (Tokyo, Taipei, Seoul) or a US gateway to Seattle-Tacoma (SEA), ~17-19h total.

peak.why: Summer: reliably dry, sunny and mild (highs ~24-27C) with long days and the clearest views of Rainier and the Olympics - among the best summer weather in the US and the reason to time a visit here. Also the busiest and priciest stretch; September stays fine with thinner crowds.

mid.why: Spring and early-fall shoulders: milder and greener (cherry blossoms late March into April, Skagit Valley tulips in April) but still changeable and often wet, sun and cloud trading off day to day. June is often grey until mid-month before summer sets in; October brings fall colour and the first sustained rain.

low.why: The grey season: frequent light rain and drizzle (November is the wettest month, January the cloudiest), heavy overcast and short days - about 8.5 hours of daylight around the December solstice - with highs only ~7-10C. Hard freezes and lowland snow are uncommon but briefly disruptive when they hit. Everything stays open in what is very much an indoor-culture city (coffee, music, museums, food), and it's the cheapest, quietest time to visit.

name: Zhangjiajie National Forest Park
description: The sandstone-pillar forest of Hunan's Wulingyuan area - thousands of quartzite spires up to 300m tall (the 'Avatar' Hallelujah Mountains), linked by clifftop trails, cable cars and the Bailong glass elevator, with Tianmen Mountain and its skywalks nearby.
travel: Seasonal direct flights Bangkok to Zhangjiajie (DYG), ~3h; otherwise via a Chinese hub (Changsha, Guangzhou, Shanghai) then a short flight or ~4h high-speed rail from Changsha. The park entrance is ~40min from Zhangjiajie city.

peak.why: Autumn: the clearest, driest and most comfortable weather of the year (15-20C), with the best odds of both sharp pillar views and early-morning cloud seas, plus foliage from late October. The top window - though Golden Week (Oct 1-7) is extremely crowded and late November turns cold in the mountains.

mid.why: Spring: mild and green with wildflowers and fewer crowds than summer or autumn, but noticeably rainier - low cloud and mist are common and can either drape the pillars beautifully or white out the views for days. Early-May Labour Day holiday is very crowded.

low.why: Summer is the hottest and wettest time (plum rains Jun-Jul) and brings the worst crowds - Jul-Aug school holidays mean hours-long queues for the Bailong Elevator and cable cars. Winter is cold with occasional snow, which is striking and near-empty, but heavy snow, ice or high wind can close the cable cars, Bailong Elevator, glass walkways and cliff plank paths and halt the shuttle buses when mountain roads shut. The park stays open year-round.

name: Almaty
description: Kazakhstan's largest city, spread along the foot of the snow-capped Trans-Ili Alatau - leafy Soviet-era boulevards, the Green Bazaar and a lively cafe scene, with hiking trails, the turquoise Big Almaty Lake, Shymbulak ski resort and Charyn Canyon all within a day's reach.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok to Almaty (ALA), ~7h.

peak.why: Summer into early autumn: the Alatau trails and roads are snow-free, the alpine lakes (Big Almaty Lake, Kolsai, Kaindy) are reachable, and September is the standout - stable, dry, golden and less crowded. The city itself is hot in Jul-Aug (30C+) and Charyn Canyon is brutal at midday.

mid.why: Shoulder months: April-May is mild and green (apple and apricot blossom, steppe tulips) but the rainiest time, with snow lingering on higher trails into June - though it's prime season for Charyn Canyon. October is crisp and golden and ideal for the city and Charyn, while the high passes and the Kolsai/Kaindy lake roads close for the season.

low.why: Winter: cold (highs around -4 to -8C), snowy, and often hazy with pollution trapped against the mountains. The city, Green Bazaar, museums and cafes carry on and Charyn Canyon is still doable if cold, but alpine hiking and the lake roads are out - this is ski season instead.

peak.why: Core ski season at Shymbulak (2,200-3,200m, ~30min from the city), with the most reliable snowpack in January-February, plus skating at the open-air Medeu rink just below. Cold and sometimes smoggy down in the city.

low.why: Season shoulders: Shymbulak usually opens in mid-to-late November and runs toward mid-April, and Medeu can open as early as late October, but snow cover is thin and weather-dependent at both ends and lower runs are often patchy.

unavailable.why: No skiing or skating - Shymbulak's slopes are bare (the gondola still runs for summer hikers and sightseers) and the Medeu rink is closed or given over to other events.

name: Switzerland
description: The Alpine heart of Europe - Jungfrau and the Matterhorn, Lauterbrunnen's waterfall valley, glacier-fed lakes and a dense network of mountain trains, cable cars and panoramic rail (Glacier Express, Bernina Express); a summer hiking playground and a marquee winter ski destination.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok to Zurich (ZRH), ~12h, then fast, frequent trains to the mountain regions (Interlaken ~2h, Zermatt ~3.5h, St Moritz ~3.5h).

peak.why: High summer: every trail is clear, even the high passes, days are long and all cable cars, huts and lake steamers run. September adds golden foliage and thinner crowds; July-August are the busiest and priciest.

mid.why: June: valleys and mid-altitude trails are green and flowery with the waterfalls at full snowmelt flow, but higher routes still hold snow into early July. October: crisp and golden lower down, though the first snows dust the peaks and the higher lifts and trails start closing.

low.why: The non-hiking half of the year. The flagship mountain railways and panoramic trains (Jungfraujoch, Gornergrat, Glacier Express, Bernina Express) run all year and the cities and lakes are fine, but Alpine hiking is out - and April-May and November are a genuine lull, with many resort-village hotels, restaurants and cable cars closed for maintenance between the ski and summer seasons.

peak.why: Core winter season: nearly every resort open, best snow depth and coverage in January-February holding through March.

mid.why: Shoulders: in April the high resorts (Zermatt into early May, Verbier, Saas-Fee, Engelberg) ski well on spring snow while most lower resorts have closed; November is thin early-season, with only glacier and high-altitude areas opening as the month goes on.

low.why: Summer glacier skiing carries on at Zermatt (year-round) and Saas-Fee (from mid-July), mostly early mornings and mainly for training, snow and weather permitting. May-early July and October are the emptiest, with essentially nothing running for recreational skiers elsewhere.

name: France
description: From Paris's museums and cafe terraces through the Loire chateaux, Normandy's coast, the Alpine peaks around Chamonix and the lavender plateaus and beaches of Provence and the Riviera - plus the wine regions of Bordeaux, Burgundy and Champagne.
travel: Direct flight Bangkok to Paris (CDG), ~12h; a fast TGV network fans out from there (Lyon ~2h, Avignon ~2.5h, Bordeaux ~2h, the Alps ~4h).

peak.why: May, June and September: mild, long days, gardens and vineyards at their best, everything open, and crowds and prices still manageable - the consensus sweet spot, May and September especially.

mid.why: April is fresh and blossoming but cooler and showery. July-August bring the longest days and festivals but the heaviest crowds and prices, and many family-run restaurants and shops close for les grandes vacances (August especially, in Paris and the countryside) while the Riviera and Provence are packed. October is golden and quieter as the harvest winds down, turning cooler and wetter.

low.why: Winter: cold, grey, short days and wetter, with rural sights, gardens and many chateau and vineyard estates on reduced hours or closed. Paris and the big cities stay fully open - museums, food, and the Christmas markets, Alsace's above all - and prices are at their lowest.

peak.why: Core winter season across the big French Alps areas (Chamonix, Val d'Isere, Tignes, Les Trois Vallees), with the best snow depth and coverage in January-February holding through March.

mid.why: Shoulders: the high, snow-sure resorts (Tignes, Val d'Isere, Val Thorens, Les 2 Alpes) ski into early May on spring snow while lower resorts have closed; November is thin early-season, with the highest resorts opening from around the 22nd.

low.why: A brief summer glacier season only: Tignes (Grande Motte, roughly 20 Jun-19 Jul), Val d'Isere (about three weeks in June) and Les 2 Alpes run limited, mornings-only glacier skiing mainly for race training and camps.

unavailable.why: No lift-served skiing anywhere in France: the winter resorts have closed and the summer glaciers are either not yet open (May) or already shut for the year (August-October).

peak.why: Full bloom across all the growing areas - the Valensole plateau in the first half of the month, the higher Pays de Sault from mid-July - the one reliable window for purple rows end to end. Also the busiest.

low.why: Edges of the bloom: in late June the Valensole plateau is just coming into colour while higher Sault is still green; by August Valensole is usually harvested but the high Pays de Sault holds colour into mid-month before its own cut.

unavailable.why: Outside roughly mid-June to mid-August the fields are cut back to low green stubble or bare earth - there is nothing purple to see.

name: Los Angeles
description: Sprawling Southern California metropolis - Hollywood, the Griffith Observatory, Santa Monica and Venice beaches, world-class museums (the Getty, LACMA, The Broad), theme parks and a deep, diverse food scene, all strung together by freeway.
travel: No nonstop from Bangkok; one stop via a North Asian hub (Tokyo, Taipei, Seoul) to Los Angeles (LAX), ~17-19h total. A rental car is effectively required to get around.

peak.why: Spring and mid-to-late fall: warm, dry, clear and comfortable (highs low-to-mid 20s C), green hills and wildflowers in spring, thinning crowds. The most settled weather of the year, after the winter rain and before or after the summer heat and fire season.

mid.why: March is pleasant and green but still the tail of the rainy season. June-August is warm, sunny, peak beach and peak tourist season with the highest crowds and prices, and 'June Gloom' keeps the coast overcast until midday from late May into early July while inland valleys get hot. September is often the hottest month, with Santa Ana heat spikes (valleys to 40C) and the start of peak wildfire and smoke season - but clear skies and great beach weather.

low.why: Winter: LA's rainy season - mild by any global standard and still mostly sunny, but the few real storms of the year cluster here - and the coolest, shortest days (highs ~19C, cool evenings). Everything stays open; gray-whale watching runs Dec-April and you can ski Big Bear and surf the same day. Quieter and cheaper outside the holidays.

name: Raja Ampat
description: The Coral Triangle's epicentre off Indonesia's Bird's Head Peninsula - the richest reef biodiversity on Earth, plus manta cleaning stations, mushroom-shaped karst islets and the lagoon viewpoints of Piaynemo and Wayag.
travel: No quick route from Bangkok: fly via Jakarta or Makassar to Sorong (SOQ), ~2 travel days each way, then a ferry or charter boat to Waisai on Waigeo or straight to a dive resort or liveaboard.

peak.why: Core dry season (northwest monsoon): calmest seas, visibility often 25-30m+, and the highest marine-life density of the year - schooling fish, reef sharks, and the Dec-March reef and oceanic manta aggregations at the Dampier Strait cleaning stations (Manta Sandy) and around Misool.

mid.why: Edges of the good season: October as the southeast monsoon finishes clearing out and April as it begins to return - still largely calm with good visibility, and quieter than the Nov-March peak.

low.why: Southeast monsoon: the wettest and windiest months (June-July heaviest, August rain on roughly half of days), with rougher open-water crossings, visibility down to 10-15m from runoff and plankton, and the reef mantas largely gone from the northern cleaning stations. Most liveaboards suspend operations in July-August and Misool's resorts close, but land-based diving in the sheltered Dampier Strait runs year-round at reduced quality and lower prices; September is the transition as conditions ease.
